		<title>Mirabilite Mounds at Great Salt Lake</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/mirabilite-mounds-at-great-salt-lake/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/mirabilite-mounds-at-great-salt-lake/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 15 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[crystal growth]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[dissolution]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[evaporation]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[In cold weather, a new geological feature has shown up at Utah&#8217;s Great Salt Lake in the last decade. These salty mirabilite mounds form terraced crystals that resemble Yellowstone&#8217;s Mammoth Hot Springs. Mirabilite is hydrated sodium sulfate (as opposed to the sodium chloride of table salt). The structures form when upwelling spring water partially dissolves [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/20191213_111805-1-scaled-1030x773-1-1024x768.jpg" title="Mirabilite crystals up close." alt="Mirabilite crystals up close." /></div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In cold weather, a new geological feature has shown up at Utah&#8217;s Great Salt Lake in the last decade. These salty mirabilite mounds form terraced crystals that resemble <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammoth_Hot_Springs">Yellowstone&#8217;s Mammoth Hot Springs</a>. </p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" width="1024" height="616" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/mirabilite_diagram-1024x616.jpg" alt="Diagram showing salty springs feeding upward through layers of mirabilite to form a mound aboveground." class="wp-image-31420" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/mirabilite_diagram-1024x616.jpg 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/mirabilite_diagram-300x180.jpg 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/mirabilite_diagram-768x462.jpg 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/mirabilite_diagram-1536x923.jpg 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/mirabilite_diagram.jpg 1652w" sizes="(max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Diagram showing how a salt-laden spring pushing upward through the mirabilite layer can then form mounds at the surface when the dissolved mirabilite recrystallizes after the water evaporates.</figcaption></figure>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Mirabilite is hydrated sodium sulfate (as opposed to the sodium chloride of table salt). The structures form when upwelling spring water partially <a href="/tagged/dissolution/">dissolves</a> the layer of mirabilite found beneath the lake bed. That sulfate-laden water rises to the surface, where it <a href="/tagged/freezing/">freezes</a> into the crystals seen here. </p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img decoding="async" width="467" height="360" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/mirabilite_main.gif" alt="A timelapse showing mirabilite mounds forming." class="wp-image-31421"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">A timelapse showing the formation of mirabilite mounds.</figcaption></figure>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">When temperatures rise above freezing, the water in the mirabilite <a href="/tagged/evaporation/">evaporates</a>, leaving behind white, powdery thenardite. (Video credit: Great Salt Lake Institute; image credit: <a href="https://geology.utah.gov/popular/great-salt-lake/mirabilite-spring-mounds/">Utah Geological Survey</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<item>
		<title>Droplets Can Climb Sugar Fibers</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/droplets-can-climb-sugar-fibers/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/droplets-can-climb-sugar-fibers/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 14 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[dissolution]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[droplets]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[surface tension]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31524</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[In nature, droplets and fibers can meet on a spider&#8217;s web, on fur, or on a dew-gathering cactus. Here, researchers explore what happens when the droplet can dissolve the fiber it&#8217;s suspended on. As the authors note, a lumberjack who cuts the branch they sit on makes a fatal choice. The droplet sees a different [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In nature, droplets and fibers can meet on a spider&#8217;s web, <a href="/tagged/hairy-surfaces/">on fur</a>, or on a <a href="/2015/12/desert-dwelling-plants-like-cactuses-have-to-be/">dew-gathering cactus</a>. Here, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/p39v-8wss">researchers explore</a> what happens when the droplet can dissolve the fiber it&#8217;s suspended on. As the authors note, a lumberjack who cuts the branch they sit on makes a fatal choice. The droplet sees a different outcome. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">As the droplet hangs on the fiber, it <a href="/tagged/dissolution">dissolves</a> the fiber&#8217;s sugar. Dense, sugar-laden water flows downward along the fiber and a replenishing upward flow goes along the droplet&#8217;s exterior. Because the sugar concentration is lower near the top of the drop, the fiber thins most quickly there.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img decoding="async" width="648" height="952" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sugar_fiber_close.gif" alt="A droplet at the end of a sugar fiber dissolves the fiber, then &quot;jumps&quot; up to the next intact section." class="wp-image-31527"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">A droplet hanging at the end of a sugar fiber dissolves the fiber and then &#8220;jumps&#8221; upward to the next intact portion.</figcaption></figure>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The droplet has capillary forces along its top and bottom, where it meets the fiber. At the top, the droplet is free to expand, wetting more fiber, but the bottom of the drop is pinned to the fiber. The excess capillary force there goes into compressing the fiber. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">As soon as the fiber breaks, the capillary force is no longer balanced, and the droplet jumps upward. If the drop and fiber are sized just right, the drop will jump upward enough to stay attached to the fiber instead of falling off. (Image and research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/p39v-8wss">S. Dorbolo et al.</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/LAaquaduct1-1024x576.png" title="The Cascades are a part of LA&#039;s aquaduct, where water from the Sierra Nevadas flows into the city." alt="The Cascades are a part of LA&#039;s aquaduct, where water from the Sierra Nevadas flows into the city." /></div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In the early twentieth century, Los Angeles had capital and political willpower, but not water. So it built an engineering marvel, the LA Aquaduct, to guide water from the Sierra Nevadas down to the growing city. Grady gets into the literal (and figurative) ups and downs of the project in this Practical Engineering video.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Although the engineering prowess of the aquaduct system is impressive, as Grady points out, the LA Aquaduct&#8217;s story is much more complicated than the engineering needed to move water between two points. It&#8217;s a story where greed, corruption, politics, cultural impact, environment effects, and climate change all intersect. (Video and image credit: Practical Engineering)</p>

					<description><![CDATA[Amphibians like toads are often indicator species for their ecosystem because they are vulnerable to changes on both land and water. In this short film, videographer Maxwel Hohn follows the migration of western toad tadpoles in British Columbia, showing their daily underwater journey from deep waters, where they can hide, to warmer, shallow waters, where [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/tadpoles6-1024x576.png" title="From &quot;Tadpoles: The Big Little Migration&quot; by Maxwel Hohn." alt="From &quot;Tadpoles: The Big Little Migration&quot; by Maxwel Hohn." /></div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Amphibians like toads are often indicator species for their ecosystem because they are vulnerable to changes on both land and water. In this short film, videographer Maxwel Hohn follows the migration of western toad <a href="/2020/02/to-beat-surface-tension-tadpoles-make-bubbles/">tadpoles</a> in British Columbia, showing their daily underwater journey from deep waters, where they can hide, to warmer, shallow waters, where they eat. Over the days and weeks of their early life, millions of tadpoles make the journey, their bodies morphing as they do. Eventually, they will hop away as toadlets. (Video and image credit: <a href="https://www.maxwelhohn.com">M. Hohn et al.</a>)</p>

		<item>
		<title>Burning Oil Spills With Fire Whirls</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/burning-oil-spills-with-fire-whirls/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/burning-oil-spills-with-fire-whirls/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 09 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[combustion]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fire tornado]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fire whirl]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[oil spill]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[pollution]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=30819</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Though they are relatively infrequent, large marine oil spills, like 2010&#8217;s Deepwater Horizon, are devastating and incredibly difficult to clean up. In many locations, the &#8220;best&#8221; option for responding to such disasters is burning off the oil before it can absorb enough water to sink. But these floating fires leave behind unburned oil and produce [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Though they are relatively infrequent, large marine <a href="/tagged/oil-spill/">oil spills</a>, like 2010&#8217;s Deepwater Horizon, are devastating and incredibly difficult to clean up. In many locations, the &#8220;best&#8221; option for responding to such disasters is burning off the oil before it can absorb enough water to sink. But these floating fires leave behind unburned oil and produce soot. To enhance the burn, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fuel.2025.136093">researchers are looking</a> at the possibility of triggering large-scale <a href="/tagged/fire-whirl/">fire whirls</a>.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Often seen in wildfires, these fire vortices are intense and localized. Researchers made a more than 5-meter tall version in these experiments by arranging three walls that spun up the in-flowing air. The fire whirl sat above a pool of water topped in a layer of oil that served as the whirl&#8217;s fuel.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Within the whirl, the fire&#8217;s burn rate was 40% higher than a typical pool fire, and soot production was 40% lower&#8211;showing that fire whirls can burn cleaner. But the whirls are more finicky to start and maintain. It&#8217;s not yet clear whether such intense whirls are possible in the chaotic conditions on the ocean. (Research and image credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fuel.2025.136093">W. Cui et al.</a>; via <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2026EO260158">Eos</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-large"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1024" height="575" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/fire_whirl_exp1-1024x575.jpeg" alt="View of a large-scale fire whirl experiment built around an oil spill on a pool." class="wp-image-30822" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/fire_whirl_exp1-1024x575.jpeg 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/fire_whirl_exp1-300x169.jpeg 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/fire_whirl_exp1-768x432.jpeg 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/fire_whirl_exp1-1536x863.jpeg 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/fire_whirl_exp1.jpeg 1600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Fixing Mosul Dam</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/fixing-mosul-dam/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/fixing-mosul-dam/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 08 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[civil engineering]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[civil infrastructure]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[dams]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[dissolution]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31068</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Keeping the water in a reservoir is an obvious challenge for any dam. But for Iraq&#8217;s Mosul Dam, it&#8217;s especially challenging because the dam was built on a foundation of gypsum, a highly water-soluble mineral. Since it was built, Mosul Dam&#8217;s water has been eating away at the underlying bedrock, making sinkholes, forcing gaps, and [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/mosul1-1024x576.png" title="Mosul Dam in Iraq was built with a critical flaw: a foundation of very water-soluble gypsum." alt="Mosul Dam in Iraq was built with a critical flaw: a foundation of very water-soluble gypsum." /></div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Keeping the water in a reservoir is an obvious challenge for any dam. But for Iraq&#8217;s Mosul Dam, it&#8217;s especially challenging because the dam was built on a foundation of gypsum, a highly water-soluble mineral. Since it was built, Mosul Dam&#8217;s water has been eating away at the underlying bedrock, making sinkholes, forcing gaps, and generally working its way out. That, obviously, creates a huge risk for dam failure and massive downstream flooding.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">To get the dam stabilized&#8211;at least to a point where Iraqi engineers could keep up with filling the holes as they form&#8211;took a massive international engineering project, carried out in the shadow of armed conflict. (Video and image credit: Practical Engineering)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<item>
		<title>The Disappearing Great Salt Lake</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/the-disappearing-great-salt-lake/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/the-disappearing-great-salt-lake/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 07 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[geophysics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[porous flow]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[saline lakes]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31410</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Since 1989, Utah&#8217;s Great Salt Lake has lost some 70% of its surface area. The exposed lakebed left behind is a source of toxic dust that gets lifted into the air. Researchers are trying to understand what water sources exist beneath the lake and whether they might save the saline lake and its ecosystem from [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Since 1989, Utah&#8217;s Great Salt Lake has lost some 70% of its surface area. The <a href="/2023/04/explaining-salt-polygons/">exposed lakebed</a> left behind is a source of toxic dust that gets lifted into the air. Researchers are trying to understand what water sources exist beneath the lake and whether they might save the saline lake and its ecosystem from disappearing entirely. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">A <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/geosciences16030114">recent study</a> pinpoints underground water by measuring the electrical resistance between electrodes placed meters apart in the ground (photo above). Because salty water is more electrically conductive than fresh water, the researchers can distinguish between them. So far, they&#8217;ve found quite a lot of fresh water, sometimes only a couple meters below the surface. But those patches are often quite close to saline water, too.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The group also described to Eos that they found mounds of invasive reeds lying atop concentrations of fresh water. The invasive species seems to be sucking up water that would otherwise feed back into the lake or support native plants that provide habitat to native birds. (Image credit: M. Thorne; research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/geosciences16030114">M. Jacketta et al.</a>; via <a href="https://eos.org/articles/whats-below-the-great-salt-lake-more-water?__readwiseLocation=">Eos</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>
					
					<wfw:commentRss>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/the-disappearing-great-salt-lake/feed/</wfw:commentRss>

		<post-id xmlns="com-wordpress:feed-additions:1">31410</post-id>	</item>
		<item>
		<title>Swirls Above the Southern Ocean</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/swirls-above-the-southern-ocean/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/swirls-above-the-southern-ocean/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 06 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[flow visualization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[gravity wave]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[lee waves]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[satellite image]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[von Karman vortex street]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31341</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[In the Southern Ocean, obstacles are sparse. But the ice-cloaked volcano of Peter I Island is tall enough at over 1600 meters to disrupt the wind. At steady wind speeds between about 18 to 54 kilometers per hour, flowing past the island creates vortices that shed from one side and then the other. The result [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In the Southern Ocean, obstacles are sparse. But the ice-cloaked volcano of Peter I Island is tall enough at over 1600 meters to disrupt the wind. At steady wind speeds between about 18 to 54 kilometers per hour, flowing past the island creates vortices that shed from one side and then the other. The result is a <a href="/tagged/von-Karman-vortex-street">von Karman vortex street</a> like the one seen here, flowing toward the upper right. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The overlaid ripple structures in the cloud layer are reminiscent of <a href="/tagged/gravity-wave/">gravity waves</a>. Perhaps, the wind&#8217;s passage made some <a href="/tagged/lee-waves/">lee waves</a> that the vortices distorted? (Image credit: M. Garrison; via <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/a-sea-of-spinning-clouds/">NASA Earth Observatory</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-large"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="922" height="1024" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/peteriisland_oli_20260211_main-922x1024.png" alt="A von Karman vortex street stretches downstream from Peter I Island." class="wp-image-31342" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/peteriisland_oli_20260211_main-922x1024.png 922w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/peteriisland_oli_20260211_main-270x300.png 270w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/peteriisland_oli_20260211_main-768x853.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/peteriisland_oli_20260211_main-1383x1536.png 1383w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/peteriisland_oli_20260211_main-1843x2048.png 1843w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/peteriisland_oli_20260211_main.png 2000w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 922px) 100vw, 922px" /></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/selfpol1-1024x576.png" title="From &quot;Self-pollination in a flower of thymeleaf speedwell (Veronica serpyllifolia)&quot; by Jay McClellan." alt="From &quot;Self-pollination in a flower of thymeleaf speedwell (Veronica serpyllifolia)&quot; by Jay McClellan." /></div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Though we rarely notice their movement in the moment, <a href="/tagged/plants/">plants</a>, and especially their flowers, are frequently on the move. Here, retired engineer Jay McClellan captures a thymeleaf speedwell flower as it opens, then pushes a stamen toward its pistil, thereby pollinating itself. Like much of the motion executed by plants, these movements come from <a href="/tagged/turgor-pressure/">pumping water</a> between different cells, swelling and shrinking them as needed to execute the overall motion. (Video and image credit: <a href="https://www.nikonsmallworld.com/galleries/2025-small-world-in-motion-competition/self-pollination-in-a-flower-of-thymeleaf-speedwell-veronica-serpyllifolia">J. McClellan</a>; via <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2025/09/2025-nikon-small-world-in-motion-video-competition/?__readwiseLocation=">Colossal</a>)</p>

		<item>
		<title>Closing a Venus Fly Trap</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/closing-a-venus-fly-trap/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/closing-a-venus-fly-trap/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 02 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[biology]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[plants]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[turgor pressure]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[venus fly trap]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31297</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The Venus fly trap has long fascinated scientists with its ability to catch fast-moving prey. Just how the plant closes its &#8220;trap&#8221; leaf so quickly is a matter of debate. A new study gives us more detail&#8211;but not complete clarity&#8211;about what&#8217;s going on. One way that plants move rapidly is by moving water into or [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The <a href="/?s=venus+fly+trap">Venus fly trap</a> has long fascinated scientists with its ability to catch fast-moving prey. Just how the plant closes its &#8220;trap&#8221; leaf so quickly is a matter of debate. A <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed5051">new study</a> gives us more detail&#8211;but not complete clarity&#8211;about what&#8217;s going on.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">One way that plants move rapidly is by moving water into or out of cells, changing their internal pressure. The new experiments showed that this is <em>not</em> what the fly trap does. Specifically, by watching the speed at which individual Venus fly trap cells take up water, the team concluded that closing the leaf would take 30-150 seconds&#8211;far more than the 1 second observed.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Instead, the team showed that the trap&#8217;s rapid closure happens because the plant&#8217;s cell walls rapidly soften, making the leaf unable to stay open against previously-stored elastic energy. Instead, the trap snaps closed. The physical mechanism behind the softening is still unclear, though, so the charismatic plant still has mysteries for us to discover. (Image credit: <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/a-close-up-of-a-bunch-of-green-plants-bEKEuv_Fiyg">N. Suzuki</a>; research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed5051">J. Ryu et al.</a>; via <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-01857-2">Nature</a> and <a href="https://gizmodo.com/scientists-finally-solved-the-mystery-of-how-venus-flytraps-snap-shut-2000771133?__readwiseLocation=">Gizmodo</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>
